title: No One Will Open the Door for You
text:
No one is going to open the door for you. Keep knocking.

Insist.

On the other side music can be heard. No. It is the telephone bell.

You are mistaken.

It is the noise of machines, an electric panting, squeals,
whiplashes.

No. It is music.

No. Someone is crying very slowly.

No. It is a sharp shriek, an enormous, very high tongue licking the
pale and empty sky.

No. It is a fire.


All riches, all miseries, all men, all things disappear in that burning melody.

You are alone, on the other side.

They do not want to let you in.

Search, search again, climb, scream. It is useless.

Be the transparent little worm, curled up, insignificant.

With your little mortal eyes, go around the block, measure with your murky,
warm belly its impregnable roundness.

You, little worm, worm-mouth, worm-ear, master of death and life.

You cannot enter.

They say.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The escalating mishearings, imperative sequence, diminutive worm imagery, and isolated closing are preserved.

title: The Earth
text:
A world like a severed tree.

A rooted-out generation.

Men with no destiny but
to shore up the ruins.


To break the sea
in the sea, like an immense hymen,
the trees rock the green silence,
the stars crackle; I hear them.


Only man is alone. It is that he knows himself
alive and mortal. It is that he feels himself fleeing
—that river of time toward death—.


It is that he wants to remain. To keep on going,
to climb, against death, toward the eternal.
He is afraid to look. He closes his eyes
to sleep the sleep of the living.


But death, from within, sees.
But death, from within, keeps watch.
But death, from within, kills.


…The sea—the sea—, like an immense hymen,
the trees moving the green air,
the snow in flames of the light held aloft…
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The repeated anaphora, parenthetical river of time, feminine and masculine sea, and closing images are preserved.

title: To the Vast Majority
text:
Here you have, in song and soul, the man
who loved, lived, died within
and one fine day went down into the street: then
he understood—and broke all his verses.


That is how it is, how it was. One night he went out
with foam shooting from his eyes, drunk
with love, fleeing without knowing where:
where the air would not stink of death.


Shops of peace, cradled pavilions,
were his arms, like flame in the wind;
waves of blood against his chest, enormous
waves of hate, look, all over his body.


Here! Come! Ah! Atrocious angels
cross the sky in horizontal flight;
horrible metal fish travel
the backs of the sea, from port to port.


I give all my verses for one man
at peace. Here you have, flesh and bone,
my last will. Bilbao, April
eleventh, fifty-one.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The direct address, violent aerial imagery, and final testament with place and date are preserved.

title: Dream Girl
text:
One day you will arrive with a frailty of love,
tender as dew,
impetuous as rain,
the bronze of the sun on your skin,
the hum
of the breeze in your murmurs,
and you will alight with the elegance of a mountain flower.


You will arrive with your slender, expressive arms,
your head tilted
in a way no sculptor has ever captured,
and shades spoken by shoulder and neck,
your
face with the will to pass and pass again,
as many times as the skies in
delicate change
of clouds and blues and flickering sun.



Except that
perhaps you will not arrive, oh dream girl,
perhaps we will only
cross paths as the world turns
and take from a glance into the eyes
a film of hope and a
day to remember.



* * *


Dreams at twilight
Dreams at twilight,
dreams only at the end of day
that, as day
falls, return
to gray things, to darkness,
to what is distant
and deep,
to the land of dreams.


Dreams, dreams only at twilight,
only old photographs,
remembered,
of lost days when the loss of day
with
tears wrote the loss of the heart.


So may tears and losses and broken dreams
find your heart at
twilight.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering of Carl Sandburg. The supplied Spanish combines the dream-girl poem with ‘Dreams at Twilight’; both headings, repetitions, and visual transitions are preserved.

title: Fossils
text:
Let the soul plunge for an instant
into the arid sea of desire
and let your bronze effigy
rise, false, from its foam.


*


Let the breeze, in its breath, stir
your black, loose hair
and, wrapped in its caress,
the mist of your body.


*


To the white bowl of your soft hands,
feverish support for my burning brow,
to the red gleam of your fine lips,
sweet caress of my clumsy mouth,
always dreamed.


You who spill a curl over your brow
when your head bends sadly,
you who frighten in your black eyes
the melancholy light and sweet shine,
you who widen a sob in your neck
and moisten a sigh on your lips.


*


A synchrony of soft sighs,
savory with brine, dyed by the sun,
molded in the brown flesh
of the virgin of the sweet
and pastoral arpeggio.



1942
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The sensual apostrophe, asterisks, and closing date are preserved; ‘resol’ is rendered as sunlight on the brine-colored flesh.

title: Maid's Bath
text:
Then she would throw
pebbles into the soapy water,
watch the violet signature of foam
dissolve,
the islands drift and join, wrapped
in a cordial smell or like a warm
memory of her laughter.


How many times could what now seems
so strange have happened?
It must have been on appointed afternoons,
at the hour of the sun,
when discipline takes a nap.


At once she would return,
her starched uniform creaking,
and look very seriously at the inhabitant
who still smiled at her
from the other side of the wire mesh.


She emptied the washbasin
over the garden gravel.
Bubbles
on the hairy skin of the geraniums…


Her splendid nakedness,
to which the branches paid homage,
I will admit was
nothing more than an aestheticist's memory.
But I would like to be younger
so I could imagine
(thinking of the imminence of something else)
that it was the vigor of the sovereign people.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The domestic scene, wire-mesh encounter, and late political turn are preserved; ‘barreño’ is rendered as washbasin.

title: And You, My Love
text:
And you, my love, do you give thanks with me
for the generous occasions the sea
gave us to be together? Do you remember,
almost by touch, as I do,
the uneasy caress between two maneuvers,
the trembling of your breasts
in the shirt open to the wind?


And the peaceful afternoons,
when the sail, weak as a dying man,
returned us home very slowly…
We were like guests of freedom,
perhaps too beautiful.


The blue of afternoon,
the wet violets that darkened the air
opened
and closed again behind us
like the door of a room
we would not have
dared to ask about.


And almost
a light touch was enough,
a distracted taking of you by the shoulders
and feeling your abandoned head,
while all around grew sad
and there on land, in the half-light,
the first lights blinked.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The intimate questions, sailing imagery, and door-like violets are preserved, with second-person pronouns kept explicit.

title: The Square Court
text:
Oh swift one, I love you.

Oh hurried fox at the edge of the dress
and sharp boundary of the insulting boot,
Artemis's knee fleeting among the stone,
I love you,
fugitive shadow on the noble staircase,
back amid trumpets on the bridge.

Oh vague ones, I envy you,
paired images in the gray
vapors of the half-closed panes,
impatient
—arriving late for appointments—
nerves of those who inhabit (the
safe, arrogant carelessness of the half-open door
and the ordering gesture of things that look).

I want almost everything:
the palace door with arms and figures,
the name of kings and the brass of the Republic.
I want your eyes, ingenuous foreigner,
and the soulless ease of the copyist.
I want this light of now. It is my desire
to be open, attentive, until I leave.
And I would like someone to tell me
goodbye,
contained, laughing through tears.


Stranger at the doors, you are not alone,
my hurried sadness accompanies you.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering of the French-titled poem. The title’s French form is rendered in English, while the rapid figures, palace imagery, and closing address are preserved.

title: Outside the Cat
text:
To be the cat,
to make an effort and be the cat
transient at dawn and at the summit
of the traveled, presumable world.


To be, outside the cat, all the cat possible
after the striped radiance of the final night
and the startled feline contraction.


To begin on the zinc at the edge of the claws,
in the sky draining the empty gutter
and in the spectral flower growing between the bars.


The cat that wakes, step by step, the old
miserable backs of a derelict factory
and the cottony air of branches to the ground
and the shaved earth of the wall to the road
and to the sonorous drum whose weight it shakes.


To be a cat outside and so complete. It seems
the world fits inside this undulating pause,
precise as a star, which calls you
and to which you will not refuse to stop, naked,
where no one would have imagined


dawn upon the crumbling wall,
pink dawn upon the gray of a cat,
with the nocturnal tips of breasts
pointing toward those thoughtful men
who arrive so slowly, walking on the outskirts.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The recursive cat imagery, industrial dawn, and surreal nude/feline transformation are preserved.

title: Because I Knew the Names of Fish
text:
Because I knew the names of fish,
even the rarest,
and those of the fishing grounds, and the marks
of distant underwater rocks,
they let me rummage in the baskets,
touch them one by one, weigh them,
and speak openly with me
of the subtle questions of the trade.


Because I understood knots and sails
and how to rig the gear,
they often took me with them;
they gave me a man's work.
I felt with pride
my hands redden at the touch of hemp,
a strong stink of tar and fish
impregnate me.
I knew almost everything of that simple life,
of that daily, primitive chance.


Only that knowledge was luxurious.
They did not know how to tell me,
or I could not understand, what it was like
in the worst days, the bitter
weeks of patience,
when the north wind
gnaws the entrails and the pupil grows tired
of searching the skies,
in the confused days,
when the sea with blurred outlines
is only like a shard of glass
half-buried in mud,
an unpleasant incident or a trap
for those who pass running
blind beneath the rain.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The speaker's initiation into fishing and the later reversal toward harsh weather and blindness are preserved.

title: I Come and Go to Your Womb
text:
I am tired,
beloved, and I am sad.
I come from the ravaged and lonely lands,
from where death bares itself and charges
at events, men, and waves.
I come,
beautiful one, from time, from life, from the day
when, with blood, it set my cluster
in the world,
and my leaves began to feel the agony
of a sky without shores and deep mud.
I am covered
with a spilled and wounded soul,
I stagger in the starless night,
and I leave on the walls of your sleeping house
my surrenders, my footprints
and my traces.
I go toward your
insides irresistibly
and ask you to come out into the air, to the roads,
to receive the doubts that assail my brow
and the steps that bring my
steps toward your songs.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The return/going motion, wounded vegetal imagery, intimate address, and repeated ‘steps’ are preserved.

title: One Would Think the Town...
text:
One would think the town,
after crossing the valley,
lost its reason
and drew itself a single street.


And so beneath the mountain range
it stationed itself feverishly like spring.


In its windows alcohol
is mixed with sun.


Its women and its flowers
speak the dialect of colors.


And the little stream that runs like a horse
drags the hens along in February and May.


Down the sidewalk pass
the priest, the cow, and the last light alike.


Here nothing of greater consequence than roses
ever happens.


As if rain threatened,
the afternoon that was blond has turned brown.


It seems the breeze
is trying out a perfume and a new turn.


A song unfolds a smile for me
and sinks a sigh into me.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The town's personification, color dialect, animal movement, and lightly comic final image are preserved.

title: On One of Those Afternoons
text:
On one of those afternoons
with no paint but that of my eyes,
I undressed you
and the journey of my hands and lips
filled your whole body with dew.


That world awakened in the afternoon,
with so many episodes without stories,
was silently flag-borne
and followed by peoples of anxieties.


Between your navel and its surroundings
the eyes of my lips smiled
and your hip,
a sphere in two halves,
brightened the moments of agony
in which my life fled toward your life.


We are so present
that the past does not count unless seen.
We are not what is hidden;
we are in the torrent of life.


Your body is the naked thing in me,
all the water running toward your jars.
Your name, your joy…
No one knows them;
not even you alone.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The erotic journey, water imagery, and paradoxical closing about private knowledge are preserved.

title: The Journey
text:
And I moved my vigorous traveler's legs
and stretched toward the blue mountain.
I carried the whole night on my Atlantean back.
The stars sang for me.


Dawn broke on the river and I crossed it naked
and, dripping the dawn, I cleft the whole mountain.
And it was the dark taste of raw cacao
when, chewing, the tapir's teeth grind it.


The light asked for a hollow to settle its account
(I carried a handful of dawn inside me).
The cedars tightened their distance, and violently
the shadow gathered the ray of light I split.


Upon the dead leaves of a hundred centuries, I camp.
I come from the mountain and made the blue sprout again.
I arch the field's horizontal into a clear circle.
The whole body I raised rises over my legs.


It surrounds the valley. I speak,
and life all around knows what I know.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The Atlantean burden, dawn crossing, cacao/tapir taste, and final expansive identification with the valley are preserved.
